draft.title: The League of Nations
card: The League of Nations was founded in 1920, after World War I, to keep peace between countries. It was set up under the peace settlement and based in Geneva.
It relied on collective security. Members agreed that if one country attacked another, the rest would act together against it, using pressure rather than a single country's force.
The League had no army of its own. It could ask members to apply economic sanctions or send troops, but each member decided for itself whether to do so.
The United States never joined, so the League lacked its economic strength. In the 1930s it failed to stop aggression, such as Japan in Manchuria and Italy in Ethiopia.
draft.remember: The League's peacekeeping depended on members choosing to act, and in the 1930s they did not.

a.q: Why was the League of Nations' system of collective security weak?
opts: It depended on members choosing to act together
It allowed only the United States to apply sanctions
It banned members from using economic pressure
It let its own army act without member approval
a.why: The League had no army, so any action relied on members agreeing to use sanctions or troops. The option about its own army is wrong because the League had no army of its own.
a.clue: Who decided whether to act on the League's behalf?

b.q: In 1935 Italy invaded Ethiopia, and League members were slow to agree on firm action. Which point from the card best explains why the League failed to stop Italy?
opts: It could not force members to act, and had no army
It had too many members to meet in Geneva
It had been set up before the peace settlement
It was run mainly by the United States
b.why: The League had no army and each member chose whether to act, so it could not make Italy stop. The United States did not run it: it never joined, which also limited the League's strength.
b.clue: Think about who could make members act.

a.best: It depended on members choosing to act together

b.best: It could not force members to act, and had no army

problems.detail: "using pressure rather than a single country's force" is unclear. It could suggest collective security ruled out military force, yet the next bullet says members could be asked to send troops. Clearer: "acting together rather than leaving it to one country".

check.summary: The facts and both questions check out, and each has one clear answer. One phrase in the card's second bullet could be read as saying collective security excluded military action, which clashes with the next bullet about sending troops.
